before.text: A private company is incorporated and has restricted share ownership rather than inviting unrestricted public subscription. Its separate legal identity distinguishes its rights and obligations from those of shareholders. Shares represent ownership interests, while directors manage the company within the relevant governance arrangements. A founder can remain closely involved in management, so incorporation does not automatically require distant or anonymous ownership. The restriction on public share availability distinguishes the private-company form from a public company; private here does not mean that the company must keep every activity secret. Official registration and ongoing obligations apply. A private company’s name ends with (Pty) Ltd. Its shares cannot be offered to the general public and are transferred only with the agreement of the other shareholders. Advantages: limited liability, more capital than a partnership, continuity if a shareholder leaves, and the founders can keep control. Disadvantages: legal registration costs and formalities, capital is limited because shares cannot be sold to the public, and shares are not easy to sell.

before.text: In Namibia, a close corporation is a legal entity separate from its members and generally provides limited liability under the applicable law. Membership ownership distinguishes it from a sole proprietor's unincorporated activity. The entity's legal position also means that its obligations should not simply be treated as the personal obligations of its members because they belong to it. The protection is subject to the law and does not remove separate personal commitments or consequences of conduct for which members can be liable. A close corporation (CC) is registered under the Close Corporations Act with a founding statement. It has between one and ten members, who must be natural persons (individuals), and its name ends with CC. It suits small businesses that want limited liability without the formalities of a company. A small maintenance business may consider the form because the owners want to organise the venture separately from their personal affairs.

before.text:
Unions can improve communication by giving managers a recognised channel through which to hear workplace concerns. Negotiated safety training may reduce avoidable injuries and absence. A clearer rota can reduce disputes and improve attendance. Employers may benefit when workers trust that complaints receive a hearing, because fewer concerns develop into prolonged conflict. Workers benefit directly from safer, more predictable employment. These gains explain why cooperation can be part of union activity alongside disagreement over pay.

There can also be costs. Industrial disruption may reduce output and inconvenience customers. Workers may lose earnings during a stoppage, while suppliers may lose orders. If a settlement raises costs without matching improvements in output or another source of finance, a firm may raise prices, reduce expansion or seek different production methods. These responses depend on the firm’s circumstances and choices. A union is not automatically harmful because it raises an employer’s costs, nor automatically beneficial because it represents employees. Compare the improvement sought with its costs and feasibility. A settlement combining safer equipment, training and a realistic pay timetable might achieve more lasting gains than an immediate demand that a struggling employer cannot sustain. A sound judgement states whose interests are being considered and over what period.

Separate an immediate effect from a longer-term possibility. A training session uses paid time now; its benefits depend on workers using the training and management maintaining safe equipment afterwards. A negotiated procedure may take effort to establish but later make complaints easier to resolve. Evidence about injuries, absence and unresolved complaints would help judge the outcome. Without that evidence, explain the likely direction of the effect and the condition it depends on.

When negotiation fails, a union may take industrial action to put pressure on the employer: a strike (members stop work), a go-slow (work continues at a deliberately slow pace), a work-to-rule (only the minimum the contract requires is done), an overtime ban, or picketing (members gather outside the workplace to publicise the dispute). In Namibia a dispute is normally referred to the Labour Commissioner for conciliation before a lawful strike can take place. Industrial action costs workers wages and the firm output, so it is usually a last resort. For the wider economy, a settlement that raises costs can add to cost-push inflation, lead firms to replace workers with machines or employ fewer people, causing job losses, or discourage investment. On the positive side, better-treated workers may be more productive and less likely to leave, and higher wages for low-paid workers can reduce inequality.

before.text:
A commercial bank provides deposit, payment and lending services to customers. Households may use accounts to receive income, make payments or save. Firms may use payment services, loans or an agreed overdraft. A loan provides borrowed funds with repayment obligations, while an overdraft permits borrowing through an account up to agreed terms. The bank considers risk, repayment capacity and its own lending conditions. An application, even one supported by a business plan, is not proof that finance has been approved.

A refrigeration repair firm may seek a loan for tools expected to be used over several years. It should compare repayments and charges with realistic cash receipts, rather than assume the bank’s willingness to lend proves the project profitable. A short seasonal cash gap may require a different arrangement. Deposit and payment services also matter independently of borrowing: a firm can need reliable ways to receive customer funds even when it has no expansion plan. Access, cost and reliability affect the benefit. This connects the institution to spending decisions in topic 4.3 and firms’ production in theme 5. Central banks oversee monetary and system functions, commercial banks serve customers’ banking needs, and stock exchanges organise securities trading. Clear distinctions allow the learner to choose the institution relevant to the stated problem.

Other services include current accounts for everyday payments and savings or fixed-deposit accounts that pay interest; cheques, debit orders and electronic transfers; buying and selling foreign currency for travellers and importers; safekeeping of documents and valuables; and financial advice to customers.

before.text:
Types of money distinguish forms in which monetary value is held. Cash is physical notes and coins. Bank deposits are balances recorded in bank accounts. Electronic means of payment include methods for giving instructions to transfer monetary value, such as a debit-card transaction or an electronic transfer. Some books call cards and transfers types of money, but the card only gives access to the balance. A device, card or instruction is not automatically an extra monetary asset in addition to the underlying balance.

Suppose a learner has N$120 in cash and N$180 in a transaction account. The stated balances total N$300. Possessing a debit card for the account does not raise that total to N$480. If N$50 is withdrawn from the account, the bank balance becomes N$130 and cash becomes N$170, before any fee. The total remains N$300: the form has changed, rather than new wealth appearing. If a fee is stated, subtract it separately. Payment choice can affect convenience, security, access and cost, so two balances with the same face value need not be equally convenient for every purchase. These practical differences explain why people may hold more than one form.

Payment records also differ from the balances they describe. A receipt showing N$60 confirms a stated transaction, but the receipt is not another N$60 held by the customer. Identify ownership of the funds after the transaction when reconciling totals.

Money is also classified into standard types. Commodity money is a good with its own value used as money, such as cattle or salt. Token or fiat money is notes and coins worth more as money than the material they are made of, accepted because the government declares them legal tender. Legal tender is money that must by law be accepted in payment; in Namibia both the Namibia dollar and the South African rand are legal tender. Bank money is deposits transferred by cheque, electronic transfer or debit order. Plastic or electronic money (debit and credit cards, mobile transfers) moves bank balances.

before.text:
Homogeneity means that all notes and coins of the same denomination are identical: the same size, colour, design and material. Because every genuine N$20 note looks the same as every other genuine N$20 note, people recognise it at once and accept it without examining each unit. Their serial numbers or small differences from handling do not matter. This standardisation removes the need to assess each payment unit in the way a trader might examine the quality of different animals or crops offered in barter.

Homogeneity is about appearance within a denomination. A genuine N$20 note and a genuine N$100 note look different because they are different denominations; homogeneity does not say they are worth the same. It also differs from anti-counterfeit protection: security features help establish whether a note is genuine, while homogeneity means genuine notes of one denomination look alike and can be accepted without inspection. Consider two sacks of produce of different quality: a buyer may value them differently despite equal weight. Identical notes and coins remove that variation in the payment object.

Their serial numbers or small differences from handling do not matter. This standardisation removes the need to assess each payment unit in the way a trader might examine the quality of different animals or crops offered in barter.

before.text:
Profit is total revenue minus total cost over a stated period. Profit maximisation means producing the output that gives the highest possible profit (total revenue minus total cost). Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue from selling one more unit; marginal cost (MC) is the extra cost of producing one more unit. While MR is greater than MC, each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so profit rises. Once MC is greater than MR, an extra unit reduces profit. Profit is therefore highest at the output where MC = MR. It differs from maximising output or sales revenue. A firm can sell more while adding costs that exceed the extra receipts. It can also reduce output and improve profit if the forgone sales would have cost more to supply than they earned. The comparison requires both sides of the calculation and a consistent period.

Suppose a cabinet maker has two complete monthly plans. Plan A gives revenue N$30,000 and total cost N$24,000, leaving N$6,000 profit. Plan B gives revenue N$35,000 and total cost N$30,000, leaving N$5,000. A yields N$1,000 more profit despite lower revenue. These figures describe complete stated plans, so the comparison is supported. If a case instead lists only material cost, do not subtract it and call the remainder profit: wages, premises or other costs may be missing. Use the information actually supplied and label a partial comparison accordingly.

before.text:
Consumer protection aims to improve safety, fair dealing, information and ways to seek redress. Buyers may find it difficult to assess quality, understand terms or challenge a seller individually. Clear descriptions, meaningful standards and relevant complaint arrangements can reduce these difficulties. Their role should be explained without assuming that every complaint receives compensation or that any proposed law is already in force.

Namibia’s official [trade ministry service charter](https://mit.gov.na/documents/41692/3037629/CUSTOMER%2BSERVICE%2BCHARTER.pdf/14730ac0-7050-c4a0-e6c5-2214123f4d9b?download=true&t=1720164760820) describes consumer-complaint investigation, awareness and trade inspection functions. There are also sector-specific channels: [NAMFISA](https://www.namfisa.com.na/consumer-protection/) describes consumer support and fair-treatment work for its financial sector, while [CRAN](https://www.cran.na/consumer-complaints-regulations/) explains communications complaint arrangements. These examples show that the relevant body depends on the product or service. They do not establish one identical process or remedy for every purchase.

In a case involving unclear charges, the learner can explain how accurate records, clear terms and the appropriate complaint route help establish what happened. A relevant investigation can improve accountability and information, but its conclusion depends on facts and the applicable framework. Do not substitute another country’s consumer statute or treat a draft bill as enacted law.

A practical educational example can keep the steps general: identify what was promised, retain the relevant transaction information and establish which sector or framework concerns the problem. Those steps help organise facts without prescribing a legal outcome. A disputed claim may involve misunderstanding as well as deliberate misconduct, so investigation has a role in distinguishing the evidence. The channel’s existence is useful access, while actual redress is a further outcome requiring facts and the applicable process.

Consumers in Namibia are protected through laws requiring goods to be accurately described, correctly weighed and measured, and safe; rules requiring sellers on credit or hire purchase to disclose the full price, interest and repayment terms, so buyers can compare and avoid over-indebtedness; the Namibian Competition Commission, which acts against price-fixing and abuse of market power; the Namibian Standards Institution, which sets quality standards; health inspectors, who check food hygiene; and sector regulators such as NAMFISA for financial services and CRAN for communications. Consumers can also complain to the trade ministry or to consumer organisations.

before.text:
Inflation can affect groups differently. A borrower with a fixed nominal debt may benefit from an unexpected fall in its real burden, while a lender may receive repayment with less purchasing power. The actual effect depends on interest, income changes and whether inflation was expected when terms were agreed. The borrower still needs the cash to make payments; a smaller real debt is not proof of easier monthly affordability. Firms can face uncertain costs and selling conditions, making planning harder, while the effect on profit depends on both receipts and complete costs.

An explanation should therefore name the affected person, the contract or income condition and the mechanism. Avoid saying inflation helps all borrowers or harms all firms identically. The cause also matters to the policy response: demand growing beyond capacity differs from an input-cost shock even if both raise the general level. This links the measurement to the causes of inflation and economic policy in 6.2. A sustained trend, a one-off relative-price change and an individual experience should be kept distinct so the learner can interpret the data without supplying their own unsupported facts.

Consequences of inflation: people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners, lose purchasing power; savings lose value if interest is below inflation; borrowers gain while lenders lose; workers demand higher wages, which may cause strikes; uncertainty can reduce business investment; and if Namibian prices rise faster than other countries’, exports become less competitive and imports more attractive, worsening the balance of payments. Mild, steady inflation can have benefits: firms’ profits may rise, encouraging investment and employment, and the real burden of debts, including government debt, falls.

before.text:
National Income is income generated by the factors of production of an economy over a stated period. The term needs its measurement basis when totals are compared. Labour, land, capital and enterprise contribute to production and receive relevant rewards under the applicable accounting arrangement. A measure of generated factor income differs from adding all cash received by households, because some receipts are transfers rather than new production income.

A household receiving a benefit does not create new output merely by receiving the payment. The transfer can support its spending, but including it again as factor income would confuse redistribution with production generation. A loan receipt likewise creates a financial obligation rather than directly measuring a factor reward. Wages paid for current production are a different kind of flow. These distinctions prevent a broad phrase money coming in from replacing an economic definition. Income methods also need to avoid double counting components and use consistent gross/net and valuation conventions. At this level, follow the basis supplied in the exercise instead of asserting that differently defined aggregates are exactly equal without adjustment. This links to GDP and GNP: the terms organise related but distinct questions about location, income flows and valuation. The data and definition together determine which total can be calculated, while a welfare conclusion still requires distribution and other evidence. A comparison should label its aggregate before drawing a conclusion. Two figures called income may refer to different boundaries or price bases, so their numerical difference alone can be misleading.

Gross figures include the value of machinery and buildings worn out during the year (depreciation, or capital consumption). Net National Product = GNP − depreciation, and this net figure is used as National Income.

The data and definition together determine which total can be calculated, while a welfare conclusion still requires distribution and other evidence. A comparison should label its aggregate before drawing a conclusion. Two figures called income may refer to different boundaries or price bases, so their numerical difference alone can be misleading.

Gross figures include the value of machinery and buildings worn out during the year (depreciation, or capital consumption). Net National Product = GNP − depreciation, and this net figure at factor cost is conventionally called National Income; market-price figures require the appropriate tax and subsidy adjustment.

before.canonical_answer: The total income earned by a country’s factors of production (wages, rent, interest and profit) in a year; it equals GNP minus depreciation.

after.canonical_answer: The total income earned by a country’s factors of production (wages, rent, interest and profit) in a year; on the conventional factor-cost basis it equals GNP at factor cost minus depreciation.

before.text:
Population size is the total number, while structure describes its composition, including age. A larger child population can increase demand for schooling and family services. More older residents can change care, accessibility and income-support needs. A larger working-age group can increase potential labour supply and demand for products. The actual effect depends on health, skills, productive resources and opportunities, not simply a person crossing an age threshold.

Suppose a population is 1.8 million and 62 percent belongs to the age group specified in a task. The number is 0.62 times 1,800,000 =1,116,000 people, or 1.116 million. Labelling it 1,116 million would create a thousandfold error. An age-group percentage also does not tell us how many actually work or depend on others. Some working-age people are studying or lack jobs; some older people work. Ratios using age bands are indicators with assumptions rather than exact records of dependency.

A larger market can support firms and more specialisation, but it also requires housing, infrastructure and investment. If real output fails to keep pace, output per person can fall. A policy judgement should identify which needs and resources change, the response time and how gains or burdens are distributed. This links population to employment in 7.2, output in 7.3 and living standards in 8.2. Do not equate more people with economic growth or assume one age structure guarantees prosperity. Population structure can also change without a large total change. A place may have similar resident numbers but a larger older share, altering the type of service demand. Another may attract working-age arrivals and need housing near jobs. Planning therefore needs composition as well as size. The economic mechanism follows the specific needs and resources, not the total alone. A planner may need separate information about where residents live as well as their ages. National totals can conceal a local school shortage or unused capacity elsewhere. Movement between regions redistributes service demand even when national population is unchanged. A supported response therefore connects the level of the decision—local or national—to the boundary of the demographic evidence and the resources that can actually be redirected.

The dependent population is people too young or too old to work (often taken as under 15 and 65 or over), who rely on the working population. The dependency ratio compares the dependent population with the working-age population: dependency ratio = (dependants ÷ working-age population) × 100. A high ratio means each worker supports more dependants, so taxes may need to rise or government spending on education, health and pensions increases. An ageing population raises spending on pensions and health care and can cause labour shortages. Rapid population growth can strain government aims: more people may be without work if jobs grow more slowly than the labour force, GDP per head falls if output grows more slowly than population, housing, schools, clinics, water and food come under pressure, and resources are used up faster. This is why a government may try to slow high population growth through education, family-planning services and incentives.
